810db6498aee: What does "Thy will be done" mean in the Big Book?
4d911035cf5f: In the program text (<0>pp. 1–164</0>) "Thy will be done" appears twice, each time as words members say to themselves: when someone offends them (<1>p. 67</1>), and through the day, "many times each day" (<2>p. 88</2>). A third form, "Thy will (not mine) be done" (<3>p. 85</3>), is part of the daily thought that keeps the reprieve going.
b4787eb01a52: The book doesn't define the phrase. What it shows is what the words do in each place: they replace anger and retaliation with asking how to be helpful (<0>p. 67</0>), and they remind us "we are no longer running the show" (<1>pp. 87–88</1>).
5858b3945442: It is tied to Step Three. Step Three's diagnosis is that the alcoholic is "an extreme example of self-will run riot" (<0>p. 62</0>), and its remedy is that "God was going to be our Director" (<1>p. 62</1>). Saying "Thy will be done" is how the book has members keep that decision in the middle of an ordinary day.
ce32abaf9138: The book also says what doing God's will looks like: "How can I best serve Thee" (<0>p. 85</0>), and it calls this "the proper use of the will" (<1>p. 85</1>), not giving up the will.
20fbb22a8d95: A search of the main text for "Thy will" finds it on four pages, all in Chapters 5 and 6 (twice on <0>p. 63</0>):
ed62f41d3743: "that I may better do Thy will" and "May I do Thy will always!"
53cf7b3f142c: The phrase is the line from the Lord's Prayer, but the Big Book's main text doesn't say so or name that prayer. See: <0>Why do some meetings close with the Lord's Prayer?</0>
fa8a5ff83b70: Step Three is the decision "to turn our will and our life over to God as we understood Him" (<0>p. 60</0>). The book first explains why: "any life run on self-will can hardly be a success" (<1>p. 60</1>). It describes the actor who wants to run the whole show (<2>pp. 60–61</2>) and concludes that the alcoholic "is an extreme example of self-will run riot" (<3>p. 62</3>). Its answer: "First of all, we had to quit playing God." (<4>p. 62</4>) "Next, we decided that hereafter in this drama of life, God was going to be our Director." (<5>p. 62</5>)
38721aa8dad7: The prayer offered as an example at that Step asks "Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will." (<0>p. 63</0>) and closes "May I do Thy will always!" (<1>p. 63</1>). The book says the wording is "quite optional so long as we expressed the idea" (<2>p. 63</2>).
0b7c637957fc: In the resentment inventory, resentment is called fatal to the alcoholic, because when "harboring such feelings we shut ourselves off from the sunlight of the Spirit." (<0>p. 66</0>) "If we were to live, we had to be free of anger." (<1>p. 66</1>) The book's course: see that the people who wronged us were perhaps spiritually sick, and ask God to help us show them the patience we'd give a sick friend (<2>pp. 66–67</2>). Then the words members said to themselves when a person offended: "This is a sick man. How can I be helpful to him? God save me from being angry. Thy will be done." (<3>p. 67</3>)
3dc00677a3db: What comes next shows what the words are for: "We avoid retaliation or argument." (<0>p. 67</0>) Then the inventory turns to our own part: "The inventory was ours, not the other man's." (<1>p. 67</1>)
730aaf6cff5e: So "Thy will be done" here is said by the offended person, about himself. It lets go of getting even and of winning. See: <0>Does the Big Book really say to pray for people you resent ("This is a sick man")?</0>
389f24973c7d: In Step Ten, after the promise that the problem of drink has been removed, the book warns: "We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition." (<0>p. 85</0>) "Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God's will into all of our activities." (<1>p. 85</1>) The thoughts that go with us constantly: "How can I best serve Thee—Thy will (not mine) be done." (<2>p. 85</2>)
5f39074e433e: Then a line that cuts against a common reading of "surrender": "We can exercise our will power along this line all we wish. It is the proper use of the will." (<0>p. 85</0>) The book doesn't ask members to stop using their will. It asks them to point it at serving.
f88d46134a4e: In Step Eleven, after the night review and the morning meditation, the book says: "As we go through the day we pause, when agitated or doubtful, and ask for the right thought or action." (<0>p. 87</0>) "We constantly remind ourselves we are no longer running the show, humbly saying to ourselves many times each day 'Thy will be done.'" (<1>pp. 87–88</1>)
e01cea0336d7: It says what follows: "We are then in much less danger of excitement, fear, anger, worry, self-pity, or foolish decisions." (<0>p. 88</0>) "We become much more efficient." (<1>p. 88</1>) And members "do not tire so easily, for we are not burning up energy foolishly as we did when we were trying to arrange life to suit ourselves." (<2>p. 88</2>)
5b1ee049917f: The chapter ends by pointing past prayer to action: "There is action and more action." (<0>p. 88</0>) The next chapter is Step Twelve, carrying the message to other alcoholics (<1>p. 88</1>).
7a7dd565ded4: It doesn't define God's will in general. Step Eleven itself speaks of praying "only for knowledge of His will for us and the power to carry that out" (<0>p. 59</0>), and the morning prayer asks to be shown "what our next step is to be" (<1>p. 87</1>). Each time it leads to an action: being helpful, asking for the right thought, serving.

c06dae8c86ea: Chapter 10, "To Employers" (<0>pp. 136–150</0>), is written by a member who had hired and fired hundreds of men before becoming an alcoholic himself. Its summary: "No man should be fired just because he is alcoholic." (<1>p. 148</1>). If he wants to stop, he should be given a real chance. If he can't or won't stop, "he should be discharged" (<2>p. 148</2>).
ad703741ff67: It asks the employer to see alcoholism as an illness, not weakness or stubbornness, and to give a sick employee who wants to recover the same consideration as other ailing employees (<0>pp. 139–141</0>).
44dafd3abb5f: Its suggested approach: be firm that the drinking must stop, don't lecture, make sure he really wants to quit, arrange medical treatment through a doctor, keep it confidential, and give him the book, without telling him he must follow it (<0>pp. 141–145</0>).
5cee8bce5c79: It warns against the opposite mistake too: covering for a man who doesn't want to stop. "You are not doing him a favor by keeping him on." (<0>p. 141</0>).
756ae5552e1c: The chapter is one member's account; the book doesn't name him. <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says only that "there is some reason to believe" Hank may have written it (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984). As an assistant manager in a large corporation, he lost three exceptional men to alcoholism, each of whom took his own life after being let go, "because I did not understand alcoholism as I do now" (<2>p. 137</2>). Then he became an alcoholic himself. He tells of trying to help a banker friend understand a fellow executive's drinking: the bank was sure the man was done, because he had taken a cure and been told it was his last chance. The man drank again and was fired; afterward the members reached him (<3>pp. 138–139</3>).
d3b15aa7417a: <0>Set your own drinking aside.</0> A moderate drinker can be more annoyed with an alcoholic than a teetotaler, because he controls his own drinking and "cannot see why it should be to anyone else, save the spineless and stupid" (<1>p. 139</1>).
87b78cedefc3: <0>Is he worth salvaging?</0> The alcoholic employee is often brilliant and quick, "imaginative and likeable" (<1>p. 139</1>). If he would be worth keeping without the drinking, should he have "the same consideration as other ailing employees?" (<2>p. 140</2>). If the reader isn't sure the man is sick and not just weak, the chapter suggests re-reading Chapters 2 and 3 (<3>p. 140</3>).
967908fc140e: <0>His past scrapes.</0> These can generally be charged "to the abnormal action of alcohol on his mind" (<1>p. 140</1>). Not all alcoholics are honest when sober, and some will take advantage of kindness. "If you are sure your man does not want to stop, he may as well be discharged, the sooner the better." (<2>p. 141</2>). The writer says being fired first, then shown the solution, might have brought him back "a well man" six months later (<3>p. 141</3>).
2d1c8d3760ad: <0>Be firm.</0> Tell him you know about his drinking "and that it must stop" (<1>p. 141</1>); you'd like to keep him, but can't if he keeps drinking. "A firm attitude at this point has helped many of us." (<2>p. 142</2>).
e1e95c7917cc: <0>Don't lecture.</0> Assure him you won't moralize or condemn, and explain alcoholism as an illness (<1>p. 142</1>).
70f2b9313ca9: <0>Probe whether he really wants to stop.</0> "Will he take every necessary step, submit to anything to get well, to stop drinking forever?" (<1>p. 142</1>). If he still thinks he can drink again, even beer, he may as well be discharged after his next bender (<2>p. 142</2>).
18789e3daff9: <0>Medical treatment, through a doctor.</0> For a man drinking or just off a spree, "a certain amount of physical treatment is desirable, even imperative" (<1>p. 143</1>), referred to the employer's own doctor. The employer may advance the cost, to be deducted later from his pay, so he feels responsible (<2>p. 143</2>). But "physical treatment is but a small part of the picture" (<3>p. 143</3>); he must undergo "a change of heart" (<4>p. 143</4>).
a559815bc3cc: <0>Keep it confidential.</0> Treat it as "a strictly personal matter" (<1>p. 143</1>), never discussed without his consent.
db59fb30a844: <0>The book, not a command.</0> Give the book to his doctor and to him; "it is best that no one tell him he must abide by its suggestions" (<1>p. 144</1>). "The man must decide for himself." (<2>p. 144</2>). The writer doesn't offer the approach "as the last word on this subject" (<3>p. 144</3>): "After all, are you not looking for results rather than methods?" (<4>p. 144</4>).
588127facab0: <0>When he comes back.</0> Be ready to hear shocking things, such as a padded expense account; his new honesty demands it (<1>p. 145</1>).
e32890e05401: Protect him from office gossip and malicious jokes about his drinking (<0>pp. 145–146</0>).
5e7be7443739: He may overwork; encourage him to play, and allow reasonable time for helping other alcoholics, which is "necessary to maintain his sobriety" (<0>p. 146</0>).
7b84a35ea294: "Your man may be trusted." (<0>p. 146</0>). If he does drink and is really trying, he'll tell you, even at the cost of his job.
c8c790ca357f: If he stumbles, you decide whether to keep him; "you should feel under no obligation to keep him on, for your obligation has been well discharged already" (<0>p. 147</0>).
65b474ae3a5e: Give junior executives the book, so they stop covering for drinking employees and can be fair and square with them (<0>pp. 147–148</0>).
fbc1015c0fe6: Many firms think they have no alcoholic problem; it might pay "to take another look down the line" (<0>p. 149</0>). The chapter is about alcoholics, "sick people," not the habitual or whoopee drinker, for whom a strict policy is "undoubtedly sound" (<1>p. 149</1>).

ca293aa47830: What does "like a tornado roaring his way through the lives of others" mean?
964238380ee7: It is a picture of the damage an alcoholic's drinking does to the people at home: "The alcoholic is like a tornado roaring his way through the lives of others." (<0>p. 82</0>). The next lines name the damage: broken hearts, dead relationships, uprooted affections, a home kept in turmoil by "Selfish and inconsiderate habits" (<1>p. 82</1>).
128f1903e894: It is there to answer one idea: the alcoholic who says that staying sober is all he needs to do. The book agrees he must stay sober, "for there will be no home if he doesn't" (<0>p. 82</0>), but calls a man "unthinking when he says that sobriety is enough" (<1>p. 82</1>).
d87112d4e3f7: What it asks for instead is amends at home: "there is a long period of reconstruction ahead" (<0>p. 83</0>), and "A remorseful mumbling that we are sorry won't fill the bill at all" (<1>p. 83</1>). The alcoholic is to sit down with the family and go over the past, without criticizing them, and then live the change (<2>p. 83</2>).
56fd074d3aaf: The line is in Chapter 6, "Into Action," in the part of the chapter about amends (Steps Eight and Nine, <0>pp. 76–83</0>). The pages just before it deal with the hardest cases at home: an affair, and whether to tell a wife about it (<1>pp. 80–82</1>). Then the book turns to everyone else: "If we have no such complication, there is plenty we should do at home." (<2>p. 82</2>). So the tornado is not about a special case. It is about the ordinary alcoholic home.
d1d7dcab7c09: <0>The excuse.</0> "Sometimes we hear an alcoholic say that the only thing he needs to do is to keep sober." (<1>p. 82</1>). The book doesn't dismiss sobriety; it says he certainly must keep sober (<2>p. 82</2>). "But he is yet a long way from making good to the wife or parents whom for years he has so shockingly treated." (<3>p. 82</3>).
2b91e1ba7a93: <0>The families' patience.</0> Before the tornado comes a line about the people who stayed: "Passing all understanding is the patience mothers and wives have had with alcoholics." (<1>p. 82</1>). Without it, the book says, many members would have no homes today and might be dead (<2>p. 82</2>).
ab0fa365f838: <0>The tornado.</0> The alcoholic tears through other people's lives. "Hearts are broken. Sweet relationships are dead. Affections have been uprooted." (<1>p. 82</1>).
f1d5ba70d3d2: <0>The farmer.</0> A man who says sobriety is enough "is like the farmer who came up out of his cyclone cellar to find his home ruined" (<1>p. 82</1>). The farmer tells his wife he doesn't see anything the matter, and isn't it grand the wind has stopped blowing (<2>p. 82</2>). The joke is that the storm stopping doesn't rebuild the house, and the farmer can't see the wreck around him.
6787af1d2cf6: <0>What to do.</0> "Yes, there is a long period of reconstruction ahead. We must take the lead." (<1>p. 83</1>). Not a mumbled apology but a frank talk with the family about the past "as we now see it, being very careful not to criticize them" (<2>p. 83</2>). "Their defects may be glaring, but the chances are that our own actions are partly responsible." (<3>p. 83</3>). So "we clean house with the family," asking each morning to be shown "the way of patience, tolerance, kindliness and love" (<4>p. 83</4>).
4e3bf4b99a00: <0>Living it, not preaching it.</0> "The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it." (<1>p. 83</1>). Unless the family wants it, he shouldn't urge spiritual principles on them or talk about them constantly: "Our behavior will convince them more than our words." (<2>p. 83</2>).
